# Frozen vertical planes in an ambient projective facet deformation

This note verifies the proposed deformation at the original integer labels. It also gives a stopping rule: on a polytope, each of its two one-sided first speeds is already an exactly realizable normal-dependent convex-field speed. A base crease can prevent those speeds from being negatives. A three-interval prism calculation distinguishes this kink from a new neutral second-order direction.

The archived `candidate 3a33d309cb62f910` explains why applying a continuous projective map while holding base labels fixed generally introduces a bilinear term. The present construction instead changes ambient planes and freezes the projection constraints. It is not that map. Its physical realization is a special case of the affine fields in `candidate 2951c303a65db1e9`; the explicit speed-closure argument below identifies why it adds no first-order normal-stress test. No mixed-measure invariance or numerical depth bound is asserted.

## 1. An actual two-sided finite-plane path

Work in the affine span of the base. Let B=conv P, P=B intersect Z^n, and let C be the canonical convex hull of its positive polytopal integer fibers. Write its nonvertical facet inequalities as

    a_r.z + u_r.X <= b_r,       u_r != 0,             (1)

and its vertical constraints as z in B. Choose an interior ambient origin; then b_r>0. More generally the proof needs only the finite representation, not positivity of each displayed intercept. Let

    l(z,X)=l_0+c.z+h.X

be any fixed affine function. For sufficiently small positive and negative t define

    C_t={ (z,X):z in B,
           a_r.z+u_r.X+t b_r l(z,X)<=b_r, all r }.   (2)

Every defining constraint is affine, so C_t is convex. Its continuous normals are u_r+t b_r h and remain nonzero for small t. The origin convention is immaterial to the proof, but the operation itself depends on the chosen affine chart.

The C_t are uniformly bounded. Indeed, boundedness of the old fibers implies that the u_r have no nonzero common recession direction. Compactness of the continuous unit sphere gives a constant c_0>0 such that max_r u_r.e>=c_0 for every unit e. For small |t| the same maximum for u_r+t b_r h is at least c_0/2. As z ranges over bounded B, (2) now bounds |X| uniformly.

Choose an interior ball in every old sampled fiber. The finitely many strict slacks at its center and bounded perturbations retain a smaller ball for both signs of sufficiently small t. Thus all sampled fibers remain positive. In particular every vertex of B has a nonempty fiber, so projection(C_t)=B. The sampled base set is exactly P. All anchored Minkowski inclusions hold because C_t is convex. Replacing C_t by the convex hull of its sampled fibers leaves those fibers exactly unchanged; this optional canonical replacement need not preserve the other real-base fibers.

There is no change of the integer labels. Neither total mixed volume nor cap masses are presumed constant.

## 2. Exact one-sided speeds, including base creases

At a surface-regular point X of K_z let n be the old continuous unit outward normal and put

    R(z,n)={r:u_r/|u_r|=n,
                  b_r-a_r.z=|u_r| h_(K_z)(n)},
    B_r=b_r/|u_r|.

This set is nonempty and is independent of X within the exposed face F_z(n). All active nonvertical inequalities at a regular fiber boundary point have continuous normal n. With s decreasing the radius from an old interior center o_z, write X_s=o_z+(1-s)(X-o_z). An active inequality is

    s u_r.(X-o_z) >= t b_r l(z,X_s).

The finite constraints also give a uniform O(|t|) radial displacement. Any constraint active at a new endpoint limits to an old active constraint. Consequently the signed inward normal velocities, each parametrized by a positive parameter, are exactly

    v_+(z,X)=max_(r in R(z,n)) B_r l(z,X),
    v_-(z,X)=max_(r in R(z,n)) [-B_r l(z,X)].        (3)

Here v_+ belongs to C_t, t down to zero, and v_- belongs to C_(-t), t down to zero. There is no extra maximum with zero. The radial proof supplies bounded a.e. speeds and the usual signed shell first variations. In particular

    M'(0+)=-sum_z int_(boundary K_z) v_+ dS,

and the analogous formula holds for v_-. Proper fixed caps have loss integral of v over their captured old boundary. Supporting fixed caps retain their actual directional hinge rule; (3) does not linearize that rule.

At a crease,

    v_++v_- = |l(z,X)|
                 [max_(r in R) B_r-min_(r in R) B_r].             (4)

Thus two-sided existence of the plane path does not imply an odd boundary derivative.

For an exact example let P={-1,0,1,2},

    K_z=[-r(z),r(z)],       r(z)=min(2+z,4-z),
    l(z,X)=z.

The four nonvertical inequalities are -z plus or minus X<=2 and z plus or minus X<=4; (0,0) is interior. At z=1 both top planes, and both bottom planes, are active. The new radius is

    r_t(1)=min(3-2t,3-4t).

At either endpoint v_+=4 and v_-=-2. All these are actual interval fibers of a convex ambient polytope with the original projection fixed.

## 3. Exact inclusion in the old normal-convex speed cone

Fix a continuous facet normal n of some sampled fiber, and set

    S_n=union_(z in P, R(z,n) nonempty) {z} times F_z(n).

In particular this union contains every measured fiber facet with normal n. A different fiber can expose only a vertex in direction n without possessing an ambient facet whose continuous normal is n; such an unmeasured face is not included unless R(z,n) is nonempty.

On this finite union of compact polytopes define v=v_+ by (3). Suppose w=sum_k lambda_k w_k belongs to S_n, where w_k belong to S_n, lambda_k>=0, and sum lambda_k=1. Every ambient plane active at w is active at every positive-weight w_k: its nonnegative affine slack on C has average zero. Since l is affine,

    v(w)
      =max_(r active at w) sum_k lambda_k B_r l(w_k)
      <=sum_k lambda_k max_(r active at w) B_r l(w_k)
      <=sum_k lambda_k v(w_k).                       (5)

The same proof applies to v_-.

There is a finite globally defined convex piecewise-affine function Psi_n agreeing EXACTLY with v on S_n. To prove this, subdivide each F_z(n) by the finitely many affine scores in (3), and take the finite vertices of all resulting cells with their v values. Define the lower convex roof of these marked vertices on their convex hull. Inequality (5) shows that every convex representation of a point w in S_n has average height at least v(w). Representing w using vertices of its own affine cell gives the reverse inequality. The roof therefore equals v on S_n. Its finite polyhedral epigraph has finitely many nonvertical lower supporting facets; the maximum of their affine functions extends the roof to the full affine span, and then to all physical space. A zero-dimensional span uses a constant extension.

Only finitely many normals n are measured on polytopal fiber boundaries. Choose continuous nonnegative functions chi_n on the unit sphere satisfying chi_n(n)=1 and chi_n(n')=0 at the other measured normals. Then

    Phi(u,w)=sum_n chi_n(u) Psi_n(w)                 (6)

is jointly continuous and finite, convex in w for every u, and has exactly the prescribed speed v at surface-almost every sampled boundary point. Its sign is unrestricted. The already proved signed canonical normal-roof deformation realizes Phi as an actual compatible speed. Repeat independently for v_-.

Thus the two frozen-projective directions give no new first-order constraint beyond the SAME signed normal-dependent convex-field cone. Equality of first speeds also retains all first-order weighted shell responses and the actual fixed-cap supporting hinges. It does not identify the finite paths or their second variations.

Equivalently, suppose a normal-preserving physical martingale transports nu to eta, with full physical row means, as in `candidate 7278f286325c46c7`. Its rows remain on every ambient support plane active at their source. Formula (5), or conditional Jensen for (6), yields

    int v dnu <= int v deta.                         (7)

This is precisely the old convex-order inequality, for each sign separately. When all active B_r agree on a patch, the two local speeds are opposite. They need not be opposite globally, so (7) cannot in general be upgraded to a projective nullity identity.

## 4. Bounded complete support menus

The same stopping rule extends to the bounded continuous complete menus already admitted by the signed-cut theorem. Let a compact index set carry continuous affine base roofs

    q_i(u,z)=b_i(u)-a_i(u).z >= h_z(u),
    min_i q_i(u,z)=h_z(u)

at all sampled bases and normals. Assume all coefficients are uniformly bounded. The cuts

    u.X+t b_i(u) l(z,X)<=q_i(u,z)

are actual signed complete-cut deformations. Their speed is the active maximum b_i(u)l. One can see its old-cone membership directly, without a polyhedral extension, from

    Phi_k(u,w)=max_i {b_i(u)l(w)
                           -k[q_i(u,z)-u.X]}.       (8)

Each Phi_k is a finite continuous convex function of w, jointly continuous in u. On the old normal bundle, the slack is nonnegative, an active index exists, and the fields are uniformly bounded. Hence Phi_k decreases pointwise to the active maximum, with a uniform two-sided bound on that bundle. Dominated convergence passes every finite stress pairing to the limit. Replace b_i l by -b_i l for the other direction. Thus even this extension belongs to the bounded-test closure of the existing cone. This is a closure statement about first response, not a measure-preserving projective map.

## 5. Exact prism test: a cusp or affine neutrality

Take n=d=1, P={-1,0,1}, K_z=[-1,1], and l(z,X)=a z+h X. The only nonvertical inequalities are plus or minus X<=1. Keeping -1<=z<=1 fixed gives

    X_+(z,t)=(1-ta z)/(1+th),
    X_-(z,t)=-(1-ta z)/(1-th).                       (9)

For |th|<1 and |ta|<1 these intervals are positive. Their centers and radii are affine functions of z. The lattice-preserving affine change of continuous coordinate

    X'=(1-t^2 h^2)X+t h(1-ta z)                    (10)

turns them exactly into the centered intervals with radii 1-ta z. This transformation multiplies every sampled volume and cap volume by the same positive determinant; it preserves their ratios. The frozen operation itself does not preserve them.

Put s=ta. For the centered family with radii (1+s,1,1-s), the middle source (0,0) has exact raw depth

    Q_0=1+2 min(1+s,1-s)=3-2|s|.                  (11)

Indeed, a nonvertical through-source cap takes half the middle interval. For the endpoint pair its opposite thresholds have total captured length at least twice the smaller radius: when both traces are proper the total is 2, and after one saturates the minimum is the fully captured smaller interval. A sufficiently large finite base tilt attains that minimum. Pure-base cuts have still larger mass. At another middle mark X' the same two steep caps give depth at most Q_0-|X'|, so the middle maximizer is unique. At either endpoint base an outward base tilt isolates an arbitrary half of its own interval, giving depth at most its radius, at most 1+|s|. Thus for |s|<2/3 the middle mark is the unique global deepest mixed point, and

    M_t=6/(1-t^2 h^2),
    Q_t=(3-2|a t|)/(1-t^2 h^2),
    beta_t=1/2-|a t|/3.                            (12)

For a!=0 this is a first-order cusp descent, already detected by the old admissible speed cone using the appropriate critical cover. For a=0 the entire family is affine-equivalent to the original prism, so normalized depth is exactly constant to every order. Although M_t and Q_t then have nonzero equal relative quadratic terms when h!=0, those terms cancel. This elementary prism has no nontrivial neutral first-order frozen-projective direction revealing a new second-order depth constraint.

For a general product B times K the same separation is exact:

    (C_t)_z=(1-ta.z) K_t,
    K_t={X:u_r.X+t b_r h.X<=b_r, all r}.             (13)

The common shape K_t is the ordinary continuous projective image X/(1+t h.X). If K is a simplex, K_t is another simplex and a common continuous affine map identifies its shape with K; only the affine radius factor remains. For other K its ordinary shape second variation can be real, but that n=0 projective direction is already archived. No general second-order exclusion is claimed.

## 6. Scope

The frozen vertical construction is valid and genuinely keeps the base lattice fixed. Its previously unrecorded bookkeeping is the crease maximum (3), the non-odd identity (4), and the exact same-speed convex extension. It does not supply a new first-order restriction on the established normal-convex stress. The second-order prism calibration is an exact bounded test, not an assertion that all second-order information is redundant. Any further use would need an explicit non-product second-order argument retaining actual cap response and all sampled volume changes.

The companion exact checker is `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_frozen_vertical_projective_cuts_defect_transport.py`.

# Frozen vertical planes in an ambient projective facet deformation

**Frozen-vertical projective first speeds lie in the signed convex speed cone**

For the source's canonical hull of positive polytopal sampled fibers, fix the finite ambient facet system and keep all vertical projection constraints fixed. In the specified fixed-lattice-label projective perturbation, uniform positive spanning and fiber inballs preserve boundedness and the sampled projection. On each regular fiber face the two one-sided first speeds are the maxima of the corresponding active affine scores. Common-normal convex interpolation, finite subdivision and angular interpolation realize these speeds in the signed normal-convex physical-field cone. The bounded continuous-menu extension is a closure assertion. At a crease the two one-sided speeds need not be negatives, and no higher-order or OC conclusion follows.

Scope limits: At a base crease the two one-sided speeds need not be negatives. This is first-order closure; it neither rules out useful higher-order effects nor yields OC.
